1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3.strategy: The traditional Closed Sicilian set-up: White fianchettoes the king's bishop, where it backs the e4 pawn and bears on the centre, and keeps the game closed instead of fighting for d4. A manoeuvring struggle follows: White builds a kingside initiative at leisure, Black counters on the queenside or with a central break.
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Fianchetto Variation

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4.strategy: The sharp alternative: the f-pawn takes control of e5 and prepares a direct attack on the kingside, with pieces developed actively behind it. The price is a loosened king's side and a slower hold on the centre, so the game turns on whether White's attack runs faster than Black's counterplay.
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4.name: Sicilian Defence: Grand Prix Attack

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.Nge2.strategy: Keeps White's options open: a closed set-up with a fianchetto, or an Open Sicilian with d4. But the closed lines are not very challenging for Black, and if Black fianchettoes at once, d4 leaves the c3 knight blocking the c-pawn, so White cannot build the c4-and-e4 clamp on d4, often White's best set-up there.
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.Nge2.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Chameleon Variation

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.d3.strategy: A modest, flexible move: it makes e4 solid and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, but it spends the move on a pawn rather than a piece and takes the sting out of White's play. Black develops freely, and White must find a plan afterwards.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g4.strategy: Pushes the g-pawn at once, before the pieces are out, hoping for kingside space. It loosens White's own king's side, lets Black choose the moment to strike back in the centre, and gets nothing concrete in return.
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g4.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Grob Attack

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.d3 g6.strategy: Black fianchettoes the king's bishop: from g7 it will press along the long diagonal against the c3 knight and the centre, while the c6 knight already holds d4. Sound and flexible, it leaves the choice between central expansion and queenside play for later.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4 g6.strategy: Black fianchettoes the bishop, which presses the c3 knight along the long diagonal, and keeps both plans alive: a strike in the centre, or queenside play with the c-pawn already advanced. White has committed pawns to the kingside, so Black can wait and choose.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6.strategy: Black answers the fianchetto with a fianchetto of their own: the bishop will press the long diagonal and the c3 knight, while the c6 knight holds d4. Solid against White's slow plan, with queenside play and a central break both still available.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.d3 g6 4.g4.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Portland Attack
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.d3 g6 4.g4.strategy: Gains kingside space at once, with g5 to follow so that Black's king's knight loses f6. It is double-edged: Black can attack the pawn straight away with ...h5, and every pawn push loosens White's own king's side before the pieces are developed.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4 g6 4.Nf3.strategy: Brings the second knight out to a square from which it watches the centre and the kingside, and backs the f-pawn's attack with a piece, so that the attack does not rest on pawns alone. White stays flexible about which diagonal the bishop will use.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal, where it already presses the c3 knight and the dark squares in the centre, and prepares castling. Black commits to the fianchetto and the solid kingside it brings, and keeps the choice between a central strike and queenside play open.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Bc.strategy: The aggressive way to place the bishop: it eyes f7 and works with the f-pawn and the knight towards a kingside attack. White commits to a sharp game, and the bishop may be harassed on c4, but the placement fits the attack best.

Shuts the bishop's diagonal to f7 and takes d5 and f5 under control, which blunts White's attacking plan; it also frees the g8 knight to come to e7 and keeps a central strike in reserve. The cost is that the d6 square loses its pawn guard.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Bc.name: Sicilian Defence: Grand Prix Attack, Schofman Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.f4 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.Bc.strategy: Strikes at e6 and g6 to tear open Black's kingside, with the e4 pawn supporting the thrust and the bishop adding pressure on e6. It gives up the e5 square the f-pawn held, and the attack is only worth it if Black's king shelter cracks.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop backs the e4 pawn and stands ready to hit the centre and the queenside along the long diagonal if the e-pawn ever advances or is exchanged. White chooses a slow build-up, and until then the bishop stays behind its own pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: The same set-up for Black: the bishop attacks the c3 knight along the long diagonal and covers the dark squares. Both sides now have solid, matching structures, and the fight is about who breaks out first and where, White on the kingside, Black on the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Supports the e4 pawn, so that the bishop and the knight no longer have to guard it, and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal. White commits to a closed centre and a slow kingside build-up, and accepts that the game is decided by manoeuvring, not by early tactics.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Solid and flexible: the pawn controls e5, opens the c8-bishop's diagonal and supports a later stand in the centre. Black can meet White's slow build-up with a pawn chain in the centre or with piece play and queenside pressure; nothing in the structure is fixed yet.

A less direct set-up: the e-pawn prepares a central strike and a route for the g8 knight to e7. But it leaves d6 without its pawn guard and keeps the c8-bishop shut in for longer, so it is sound but slower to create pressure than the main line.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: The attacking continuation: the f-pawn claims e5 and kingside space, with the knight to develop behind it and short castling to follow. It commits White to a kingside attack and weakens the squares behind the pawn, so the king's safety rests on the attack running faster than Black's counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Develops the bishop with a view to Qd2 and perhaps long castling, and takes d4 under control so that a black knight cannot settle there for free. It is the more positional path: White builds up pieces before deciding what to do with the kingside pawns.

The quiet developing alternative: the knight goes to e2 so that the f-pawn can still advance later and White can castle short. It gives up the control of e5 that a knight on f3 would exert, so Black can take the centre with the e-pawn at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Botvinnik Defence, with f4
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Black strikes in the centre at once, hitting the f4 pawn and claiming space with the d6-e5 chain. The g7-bishop is blunted for the moment by its own pawn, but the central tension gives Black real counterplay against White's kingside plans.

1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.name: Sicilian Defence: Closed, Botvinnik Defence, with Nge2
1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.d3.strategy: Takes the centre while White's f-pawn is still at home: the d6-e5 chain holds space and makes the f-pawn's advance costly, since the e-pawn controls f4. The price is the g7-bishop stopped by its own pawn and a d5 square that no black pawn guards.

Develops the bishop towards Qd2 and long castling and takes d4 under control. The cost is that the bishop then stands where a black knight can challenge it, so White has to be ready to give up the dark-squared bishop.

The knight takes the central post and invites the e3-bishop to trade. If White trades, ...cxd4 gains time against the c3 knight and leaves Black a pawn in the centre; if White does not, the knight stays and cramps White's development.
